If we’re talking about baking a soufflé so that it doesn’t collapse, that’s a different set of parameters. If we’re talking about the chemistry of the soufflé batter that’s gonna be something different too. And I’m sure we can think of other examples… We’re probably not going to do nuclear fusion with a soufflé, but the point is it’s a material and the relevant analytical framework needs to take into account What the material is, how it’s structured , how it relates to other things. We also need to get into the habit of remembering that our responsibility, all of our responsibilities is to the truth and accuracy. Framing things as proofs presumes a correct outcome and LLM training encourages reaching that correct outcome. Which is almost the exact opposite of the reasoning that is necessary to do a proof. Scientific reasoning, involves asking oneself how it might be wrong, and letting the certainty we have on some things force us into a conclusion elsewhere. So, if the equations fail, it is of Paramount importance to let them fail. The last thing we want is a theory built on mathematical optimism, full of meaningless equations that we’ve tweaked into the right answers without looking closely enough. Things like that may make sense in a system made essentially of springs, and dynamic tensions may very well come into play. But that’s bad science. If there is this kind of play in the system, then we need to figure out how to characterize it precisely so that we know exactly how it should be applied and we know exactly the way it should affect the outcome of an equation, so that we can see whether it is being applied consistently or whether it is being applied as a corrective to a faulty, underlying mathematical backbone. Not because those are not necessarily good things to strive for. But in my observation, it can be very easy to state something, and by stating it convince ourselves that it’s true. That undermines are thinking. We need to instead approach each problem on its own terms, in its own context, and understand and characterize what matters in an appropriate way on a case by case basis. When we try to put our thinking into templates, we miss the things that don’t fall into those templates.
